greek: Αὕτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως ἀνθρώπων· ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν Αδαμ, κατʼ εἰκόνα θεοῦ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν·
hint: The book's second heading, after 2:4 — and the opening words of Matthew's Gospel.

notes.text: The heading of 2:4, word for word as far as γενέσεως. Matthew 1:1 opens the New Testament with the same two nouns: Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ. βίβλος is first *the inner bark of the papyrus*; *a book* is its third sense.

[[flag]] The Hebrew has *ʾādām* both times: *the book of the generations of ʾādām*, *in the day God created ʾādām*. The Greek reads the first as the common noun, in the plural, *of men*, and the second as the name.

The words of 1:27, where the Greek has τὸν ἄνθρωπον for τὸν Αδαμ. [[flag]] The Hebrew here is *bidmût ʾĕlōhîm*, *in the likeness of God*: *dĕmût*, which 1:26 rendered ὁμοίωσις, is εἰκών here, the word 1:26–27 keep for *ṣelem*, *image*.
[[flag]] The Hebrew has *bĕrōʾ … ʿāśâ*, *created … made*. The Greek has ποιέω for both, as for *bārāʾ* at 1:1.

κατά with the accusative, *according to*. The entry heads its cases together and opens *down*, so *down* is the headword, as at 2:8 and 2:18. εἰκών is *a likeness, image, portrait*, then *an image in a mirror*, *a phantom*, *a simile*: from ἔοικα, *to be like*.
The 1950 printing reads ἀνθρπώπων, with a stray π, a misprint for no word; the transcription corrects it. The 1935 first printing, which is lending-only, could not be checked.
Glossed again, first in this chapter.

reading: [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[the inner bark of the papyrus|the inner bark of the papyrus, the bark, the book]] [[of origin|of origin, of source, of productive cause, of beginning, of manner of birth, of race and descent, of production and generation, of creation and the created things]] [[of men|of men, of human beings]]; in which [[day|the day, the day-break, the time]] [[made|fashioned, wrought, manufactured, produced, performed, and brought to a finished and accomplished state]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]] [[name:Αδαμ]], [[down|down, downwards, down from, down upon, over, upon]] [[a likeness|a likeness, an image, a portrait, an image in a mirror, a semblance and phantom, an image in the mind, a similitude and simile]] [[of God|God's own, divine in character]] [[made|fashioned, wrought, produced]] him;

greek: ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτοὺς καὶ εὐλόγησεν αὐτούς. καὶ ἐπωνόμασεν τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῶν Αδαμ, ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς.
hint: Male and female are given one name, Adam: in Hebrew the word for humankind.

notes.text: The last words of 1:27, repeated. Jesus quotes them in Matthew 19:4 and Mark 10:6, ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς, in the answer on divorce. Both adjectives are neuter; αὐτούς is masculine.
ἄρσην is *male*, then *masculine, strong*. θῆλυς is *female*, then, in a second group, *fresh, refreshing* (of dew), *tender, delicate* and *soft, yielding*.
[[flag]] The Hebrew is *bĕrāʾām … bĕyôm hibbārĕʾām*, *he created them … in the day they were created*: its second verb is passive. The Greek has the active ἐποίησεν αὐτούς both times.
[[flag]] The Hebrew *wayyiqrāʾ ʾet-šĕmām ʾādām*, *called their name ʾādām*, uses the common noun, *humankind*. The Greek transliterates, and the two are given one proper name.
Without the augment Rahlfs prints at 2:3, ηὐλόγησεν. *To speak well of*; *to bless* is the entry's fourth gloss.

reading: [[male|male, the male sex, masculine and strong, mighty]] and [[female|female, the female sex and womankind, belonging to women, feminine, fresh and refreshing, tender and delicate and gentle, soft and yielding and weak]] [[made|fashioned, wrought, produced]] them and [[spoke well of|spoke well of, praised, honoured, blessed]] them. and [[gave a surname|gave a surname, named, called, pronounced]] [[the name|the name, the fame, the mere name, the phrase and expression]] of them [[name:Αδαμ]], in which [[day|the day, the day-break, the time]] [[made|fashioned, wrought, produced]] them.

greek: ἔζησεν δὲ Αδαμ διακόσια καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη καὶ ἐγέννησεν κατὰ τὴν ἰδέαν αὐτοῦ καὶ κατὰ τὴν εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐπωνόμασεν τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Σηθ.
hint: The Greek numbers are not the Hebrew's: Adam begets Seth at 230, not 130.

notes.text: *Two hundred and thirty.* [[flag]] The Hebrew has 130, and 800 at 5:4. Down to Enoch the Greek adds a hundred years before each son's birth and takes a hundred from the years after it, except at Jared, where the two texts agree; each lifetime comes out the same. Methuselah and Lamech differ otherwise (5:25, 5:28).
Aorist, as every verb of the genealogy's frame is — ἔζησεν, ἐγέννησεν, ἀπέθανεν: each span of years is one completed whole.

notes.lemma: κατὰ τὴν ἰδέαν αὐτοῦ καὶ κατὰ τὴν εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ
notes.text: [[flag]] The Hebrew is *bidmûtô kĕṣalmô*, *in his likeness, according to his image*. *dĕmût* is ἰδέα here, *form*, *the look of a thing*: a third Greek word for it, after ὁμοίωσις at 1:26 and εἰκών at 5:1. The Greek repeats κατά and joins the two with καί.
γεννάω, *to beget, engender*, of the father. Neither text gives it an object here: *begot according to his form*.
Middle Liddell gives each numeral one sense, and ἔτος one, *a year*, so every number and every *years* in the chapter is plain text.
Hebrew *Šēt*; see 4:25.

reading: [[but|but, however, whereas, on the other hand]], [[lived|lived, was in full life and strength, was fresh and strong]] — one completed act seen whole, not a process observed in progress — [[name:Αδαμ]] two hundred and thirty years and [[begot|begot, engendered, brought forth, produced]] [[down|down, downwards, down from, down upon, over, upon]] [[the form|the form, the look, the outward appearance, the kind and sort and nature, the mode and fashion, the class and species]] of him and [[down|down, downwards, down from, down upon, over, upon]] [[the likeness|the likeness, the image, the portrait, the image in a mirror, the semblance and phantom, the image in the mind, the similitude and simile]] of him and [[gave a surname|gave a surname, named, called, pronounced]] [[the name|the name, the fame, the mere name, the phrase and expression]] of him [[name:Σηθ]].

greek: ἐγένοντο δὲ αἱ ἡμέραι Αδαμ μετὰ τὸ γεννῆσαι αὐτὸν τὸν Σηθ ἑπτακόσια ἔτη, καὶ ἐγέννησεν υἱοὺς καὶ θυγατέρας.
hint: 'Sons and daughters': the words each generation's second verse closes with.

notes.text: [[flag]] The Hebrew has 800.
*The days came to be seven hundred years*: γίνομαι with the years as its predicate, in the nominative.
μετά with the articular infinitive, *after his begetting*, with αὐτόν its subject. The accusative's *after* comes late in the entry, which opens *into the middle of*, as at 4:3.
υἱός, *a son*, and θυγάτηρ, *a daughter*, have one sense each, so both are plain text.

reading: [[but|but, however, whereas, on the other hand]], [[came into being|came to be, arose, were brought into existence]] [[the days|the days, the day-breaks, the times]] of [[name:Αδαμ]] [[into the middle of|into the middle of, coming among, in pursuit and quest of, after]] [[to beget|to beget, to engender, to bring forth, to produce]] him [[name:Σηθ]] seven hundred years, and [[begot|begot, engendered, brought forth, produced]] sons and daughters.

notes.text: 930, as in the Hebrew. Rahlfs prints the later spelling with -νν-; Middle Liddell heads the entry ἐνακόσιοι.

greek: καὶ ἐπωνόμασεν τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Νωε λέγων Οὗτος διαναπαύσει ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων ἡμῶν καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν λυπῶν τῶν χειρῶν ἡμῶν καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς, ἧς κατηράσατο κύριος ὁ θεός.
hint: The Hebrew explains Noah's name by comfort; the Greek, by rest.

notes.text: [[flag]] The Hebrew explains *Nōaḥ* with *yĕnaḥămēnû*, *he will comfort us*, from *nāḥam*. The Greek has διαναπαύω, *to allow to rest*: the sense of *nûaḥ*, *to rest*, to which the name is usually connected. In neither language does the verb sound like the name.
Middle Liddell has only the middle, διαναπαύομαι, *to rest awhile*. LSJ gives the active: *to allow to rest awhile*, *to interrupt*, *to relieve*.
λύπη, *pain of body*, the word of 3:16–17; at 3:17, as here, it renders *ʿiṣṣābôn*.
[[flag]] The Hebrew *min-hāʾădāmâ*, *from the ground*, has no *and* before it, and says where the toil comes from. The Greek adds καί, and the earth becomes a third thing named.
καταράομαι, *to call down curses upon*; the curse is 3:17, ἐπικατάρατος ἡ γῆ. ἧς takes the case of γῆς.
[[flag]] The Hebrew has *YHWH* alone; the Greek has κύριος for the name, and adds ὁ θεός.
Hebrew *Nōaḥ*. Luke 3:36 has Νῶε.
Capitalised because it opens direct speech, as Rahlfs prints it; listed in `speech` so the checks do not take it for a proper name.

reading: and [[gave a surname|gave a surname, named, called, pronounced]] [[the name|the name, the fame, the mere name, the phrase and expression]] of him [[name:Νωε]] [[saying|saying, speaking, declaring, calling by name, telling]] [[this|this, the nearer, what follows]] [[will allow to rest awhile|will allow to rest awhile, will interrupt, will relieve, will rest awhile]] us [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[of the works|of the works, of the business, of the deeds]] of us and [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[of the pains of body|of the pains of body, of the distresses and sad plights, of the pains of mind, of the griefs]] [[of the hands|of the hands, of the hands and arms, of the arms]] of us and [[from|from, away from, far from, apart from]] [[of the earth|of the land, of the dry ground, of the terrestrial realm]], of which [[called down curses upon|called down curses upon, imprecated upon, cursed and execrated, uttered imprecations]] [[lord|lord, master, the one having power and authority over]] [[the God|he who is God definitively, the one the article marks out, the known and the only]].

greek: Καὶ ἦν Νωε ἐτῶν πεντακοσίων καὶ ἐγέννησεν Νωε τρεῖς υἱούς, τὸν Σημ, τὸν Χαμ, τὸν Ιαφεθ.
hint: The Greek counts Noah's sons before naming them; the Hebrew only names them.

notes.text: Genitive of age, *of five hundred years*; the Hebrew idiom is *a son of five hundred years*. The number is the same.
[[flag]] Not in the Hebrew here, which gives the three names alone; *three sons* is the Hebrew's wording at 6:10.
Hebrew *Šēm*, *Ḥām*, *Yepet*. Luke 3:36–38 runs this line backward from Σήμ to τοῦ Ἀδὰμ τοῦ θεοῦ, spelling Καιναν and Ιαρεδ Καϊνάμ and Ἰάρετ.

reading: And was, and kept on being as a standing and continuing condition and not a momentary one, [[name:Νωε]] of five hundred years and [[begot|begot, engendered, brought forth, produced]] [[name:Νωε]] three sons, [[name:Σημ]], [[name:Χαμ]], [[name:Ιαφεθ]].
